28.0.s.en: (1) A cry for deliverance from the wicked

28.0.0.en: 1- "Unto thee will I cry, O Lord my rock; be not silent to me: lest, if thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit."

28.0.1.en: Be deaf (tatasamam): to make yourself deaf toward me, that is, to refuse to hear my prayer.

28.0.2.en: 1- David's crying out shows how much he needs God, for he does not merely speak but cries out, declaring his severe distress. At the same time it shows his boldness before God, for he stood before Him and cried out, showing all his feelings and needs.

28.0.3.en: 2- David trusts that God is his rock, that is, his strong refuge to whom he flees, and he trusts that no one can harm him while he is in God's protection; rather, whoever tries to strike against the rock will be broken, and if the rock falls upon him it will crush him. Therefore David is at peace as long as he takes shelter in his God, his rock. This also confirms his boldness before God, for God is not merely a rock, but his rock.

28.0.4.en: 3- When David fell into sin through his adultery with the wife of Uriah the Hittite, he humbled himself before God in repentance and asked Him not to reject his prayer and stop His ears to it, but to forgive him; and at the same time he continued to pray, and to weep, and to make his bed swim every day.

28.0.5.en: 4- David believes that God is his life, so that if God refuses to hear his prayer he will be like those who go down into the pit, that is, he is exposed to death if God abandons him. Therefore he begs God to hear him, that he may live before Him.

28.1.0.en: 2- "Hear the voice of my supplications, when I cry unto thee, when I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle."

28.1.1.en: The oracle (sanctuary): this is the Holy of Holies, where the ark of the covenant of God is found in Solomon's temple, and into which the high priest enters once every year. The oracle declares the presence of God.

28.1.2.en: 1- David's prayer is a supplication to God. Supplication means humility and contrition before God, and at the same time faith in the God to whom he makes supplication, that he may ask for His help.

28.1.3.en: 2- David's crying out to God shows the extent of his need and suffering; indeed, he finds no deliverer except God. Therefore his prayer is strong and reaches the bosom of God.

28.1.4.en: 3- The oracle had not yet been built by the hand of Solomon, but God had promised David that his son would build the temple. David prepared what was needed for building the temple, including the oracle. The oracle corresponds to the Holy of Holies in the tabernacle of the congregation, and in it is the most important thing in the tabernacle, or temple, namely the ark of the covenant of God, which declares His presence in the midst of His people. David saw this oracle by faith and lifted up his hands toward it, that is, he lifted up his hands toward God, asking for His help.

28.1.5.en: 4- Lifting up the hands is a declaration of asking for help from heaven, where God dwells; so lifting up the hands toward the oracle is asking for succor and strength from God the Savior.

28.1.6.en: 5- Moses lifted up his hands in the form of a cross before God in prayer, and Joshua was able to defeat the mighty army of Amalek. By the cross and prayer the spiritual person can overcome all the warfare of the demons.

28.1.7.en: 6- David, driven out from the face of Absalom, had his heart attached to the ark of the covenant of God. He believes in, and feels, the presence of God even when he is far from the ark of the covenant, confirming the importance of mental prayer, even if a person is not able to be in the temple of God, or the Church, because of circumstances that prevent him.

28.2.0.en: 3- "Draw me not away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, which speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts."

28.2.1.en: 1- David pleads with God not to remove him from Himself and draw him away from His bosom, lest he join the wicked and the workers of iniquity; for he cannot imagine himself except in the hands of God, whom he loved with all his heart.

28.2.2.en: 2- Although David was pursued by Saul and was sometimes compelled to be among the pagans in flight from Saul, he lived holding fast to God's commandments and attached to His house. So he asks God not to count him and number him with the wicked, because he is still His son and holds fast to his faith.

28.2.3.en: 3- These wicked men are deceivers; they speak peace with people while evil is in their hearts. David holds fast to the purity of his heart, and declares to God that he needs His help to remain in this purity, far from the hypocritical wicked.

28.2.4.en: 4- This verse is a prophecy about Christ the righteous and holy One, who was numbered with the transgressors when He bore the sufferings and the crucifixion for our sake. So He asks the Father not to leave Him, because He bears the sins of the whole world upon His head, and He is crucified for our redemption, when He said, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Ps 22:1).

28.2.5.en: 5- Perhaps David saw by the spirit of prophecy Judas Iscariot the traitor, who spoke peace with his Master, kissed Him, and delivered Him to the Jews, and they arrested Him. So David asks that God not count him with Judas and with all the traitors and the deceitful wicked.

28.3.0.en: 4- "Give them according to their deeds, and according to the wickedness of their endeavours: give them after the work of their hands; render to them their desert."

28.3.1.en: 1- David asks that the wicked be repaid according to their deeds and their wicked hearts, and not according to their smooth words that utter deceitful peace, for God is the searcher of hearts and reins; so that the wicked may fear God, and repent, and return to Him when He disciplines them, because discipline makes them feel the hardness of their hearts and the evil of their works, and so they repent.

28.3.2.en: 2- Divine justice appears in repaying the wicked and punishing them, so that the believers may be firm in their faith and upright conduct, and may not be troubled by the temporary, material success of the wicked in the world.

28.3.3.en: 3- When the Lord returns a man's works upon his head, people fear in their conduct and do not wrong others, lest all the evil they have done come upon them.

28.3.4.en: 4- David shows God's hatred of evil by speaking of the wicked's deeds, their work, and their dealings, so that people may turn away from evil in all its forms in all their conduct.

28.4.0.en: 5- "Because they regard not the works of the Lord, nor the operation of his hands, he shall destroy them, and not build them up."

28.4.1.en: 1- The sin of the wicked is that they did not pay attention to the works of God, and consequently did not believe in Him or walk by His commandments, so they deserved destruction, as the Scripture says, "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge" (Hos 4:6).

28.4.2.en: 2- The works of the Lord and the operation of His hands are His care for mankind, His support of the righteous, His displeasure with the wicked, and His governance of all His creatures. When a person contemplates all of this, he believes in God and submits to His commandments.

28.4.3.en: 3- God is grieved by these wicked men and hates their evils, so He destroys these evils, that perhaps the wicked may repent. And if they do not repent, He destroys them and brings them to an end in eternal torment.

28.4.4.en: 4- God destroys the wicked and does not rebuild them if they persist in sin. Consequently, because they refused to know God, they deserve this perpetual destruction, that is, eternal perdition.

28.4.5.en: 5- These wicked men are deceivers; they deceived people with false words of peace while concealing evil toward them. This deceit came upon their own heads, for they themselves were deceived and departed from upright conduct, and so they perished.

28.4.6.en: If you face any distress, hasten to God who loves you and cry out to Him, confident that He hears you, even if you are in the depth of distress; indeed, He will deliver you from the hands of the wicked and give you peace and joy.

28.5.0.en: 6- "Blessed be the Lord, because he hath heard the voice of my supplications."

28.5.1.en: 1- David asked in faith and cried out to God at the beginning of the psalm, and now also in faith he lifts up his heart in thanksgiving to God who answered him.

28.5.2.en: 2- David felt this thanksgiving before God answered, because he believed that He would answer; then he continued to thank Him until He actually answered.

28.5.3.en: 3- How beautiful that David remembered to thank God for His answer and to bless Him, for this strengthens David's faith and makes him feel God's presence with him, so that his joy increases.

28.6.0.en: 7- "The Lord is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth; and with my song will I praise him."

28.6.1.en: My shield: my protection and my fortress; for the shield is an instrument of war that the soldier used in ancient times to defend himself. It is a piece of wood with a handle at the back, in which the soldier places his hand, and he moves it before his head and body, so that it protects him from arrows.

28.6.2.en: 1- David's faith in the power of God made him trust in Him and not in anything else, so he felt strength and protection in Him while he was a fugitive and pursued. And since God saw his faith, He gave him victory. Victory is sure for everyone who believes in God with all his heart.

28.6.3.en: 2- Since David trusted in God, he felt victory in Him before it happened, and he rejoiced in God's being with him, and this gladness spread through all his inner feelings, that is, his heart and consequently his mind, and it also showed on his face.

28.6.4.en: 3- To express his joy, David thanked God and praised Him with a song, that is, he continued in thanksgiving and praise for a long time.

28.6.5.en: 4- Since David felt joy in his heart, and the cause of this joy was the presence of God, in whom he trusted and who gave him victory, gladness became constant in his heart, and he expressed it in constant praise, so that God became his song, that is, his heart was attached to God, and he no longer had any joy except in Him.

28.7.0.en: 8- "The Lord is their strength, and he is the saving strength of his anointed."

28.7.1.en: 1- This expresses the power of the Father's work with those who believe in Him, for he says the Lord is their strength, for He is their glory and their greatness. And it expresses the work of the Son with the believers by saying, "the saving strength of his anointed," that is, that Christ is their Savior, who will accomplish their redemption in the fullness of time on the cross.

28.7.2.en: 2- Christ the Savior gives those who believe in Him a strong and sure salvation, which he likens to a fortress, that is, the devil cannot penetrate it with all his power, his wiles, and his varied warfare; rather, the believers within the fortress enjoy fellowship with their Christ and rejoice with Him.

28.7.3.en: 3- So David cannot separate himself from the company of the believers, that is, the Church; he says that the Lord is "my strength" in (v. 7), but David wants to feel his union with the rest of the believers, so he says that "the Lord is their strength" in (v. 8).

28.7.4.en: 4- The mighty God saved David His anointed, that is, the one anointed king over his people, and became a fortress for him, protecting him all his days from his enemies; this represents the saving power of God, constant in its protection of David.

28.8.0.en: 9- "Save thy people, and bless thine inheritance: feed them also, and lift them up for ever."

28.8.1.en: 1- David changes from a man who cries to God and asks His help to save him from his enemies, into a responsible king and an intercessor for his people, asking salvation for them. By relying on God he was reassured and felt sure victory. And his bond with the company of the believers made him unable to bear receiving salvation alone; rather, he wants all the believers to receive salvation. This confirms his oneness with his people, and as a king he hands over the full responsibility to God with complete confidence in God's faithfulness to His people.

28.8.2.en: 2- He is not content to ask salvation for his people, but with the boldness of love he asks God to bless them also, giving them material and spiritual blessings, that they may enjoy fellowship with Him.

28.8.3.en: 3- The salvation that David asks of God for his people includes two things:

28.8.4.en: a - Deliverance from enemies, that is, the nations around them.

28.8.5.en: b - Deliverance from spiritual enemies, that is, the demons and all the sins connected with them.

28.8.6.en: 4- With boldness David says to God that those who believe in Him are His people and He is their God who is responsible for them, who cannot possibly abandon them. Rather, they are His inheritance, that is, the best of what He possesses; for God said, "and my delights were with the sons of men" (Prov 8:31).

28.8.7.en: 5- The third request that David asks of God for his people is that He feed them. This includes many things, the most important of which are:

28.8.9.en: b - Their spiritual sufficiency by knowing Him and cleaving to Him, and nourishing them with His Body and Blood in the Church of the New Testament.

28.8.11.en: d - Guiding them in all their steps, until they reach the Kingdom.

28.8.12.en: 6- The fourth and last request in David's intercession for his people is that God lift them up. This represents love at the highest level, so that the people of God are in His hands, and He brings them across the wilderness of this world until they reach eternal life. And when He carries them He gives them the enjoyment of fellowship with Him, and this is something that extends from earth to heaven, that is, it lasts forever with those who believe in God.

28.8.13.en: 7- God's carrying His people means lifting them above material attachments and above every sin, so that they become heavenly, spiritual, lovers of virtues. And He lifts them up even more during tribulations, so that they feel peace however great the sufferings.

28.8.14.en: How beautiful it is that you see God's work in your life and feel it, so that your heart is moved to praise Him, and you enjoy His fellowship as a result; indeed, God becomes the song of your life, in whom you find your constant joy and your hope in all the circumstances of life, however hard they may be.

28.8.15.en: The voice of the Lord: "Give unto the Lord, O ye sons of God" (v. 1). Introduction:

28.8.16.en: 1- Its author: he is David the prophet, as appears from the title of the psalm in the Beirut edition.

28.8.18.en: a - Before the tent of the ark: the first opinion is that David said this psalm after he brought the ark of the covenant of God back to Jerusalem and placed it in a tent made for it, which is different from the tabernacle of the congregation that was at Gibeon, which contained the other parts of the tabernacle apart from the ark. So after placing the ark in its own tent, David went out and recited this psalm. In the Septuagint, we find in the title of this psalm "for the going out of the tabernacle," and what is meant by the tabernacle is the tent in which David placed the ark of the covenant.

28.8.19.en: b - At the Feast of Tabernacles: specifically on its eighth day, because the Septuagint mentions that it is said at the Feast of Tabernacles, when the last harvests are gathered in the autumn.

28.8.20.en: c - At the Feast of Pentecost: that is, the Feast of Weeks, when the harvests are gathered. This feast comes fifty days after the Passover, and this opinion is mentioned in the Jewish Talmud.

28.8.21.en: d - Some think that a violent storm blew from the mountains of Lebanon in the north and passed through the land of the Jews, accompanied by lightning, thunder and fire that burned some places, so that fear and terror came upon the Jews. So David wrote this psalm declaring the power of God.

28.8.22.en: 3- Outside the tabernacle: this title found in the Septuagint carries many symbolic meanings, among them:

28.8.23.en: a - The Jews' going out from the tabernacle of Jewish faith, from following God and accepting Christ, and the Gentiles' entering into faith in Christ.

28.8.24.en: b - The soul's going out from the body, and this means preparing for eternal life by living with God and offering Him sacrifices of love, so that we are not troubled when standing before the just Judge.

28.8.25.en: c - Keeping the Church holy in the world, so that she may go out from it and be glorified in the Kingdom of Heaven.

28.8.26.en: 4- It was prayed with this psalm to ask God for rain to break a period of drought, as the prophet Zechariah said (Zech 14:16-18).

28.8.27.en: 5- There is a relation between this psalm and the one before it, which is a cry to God, and He answers with this psalm. It presents the voice of the Lord with power, so that He reassures His children and blesses them.

28.8.28.en: 6- This psalm proclaims the voice of God and repeats it seven times, confirming God's presence through nature; it is a psalm that makes us feel the presence and greatness of God.

28.8.29.en: 7- This psalm is found in the prayer of the Third Hour in the Agpeya, where we see the descent of the Holy Spirit, who descended at this hour accompanied by the blowing of a wind. And this psalm speaks to us of the mighty voice of God, which subdues nature and changes souls by the work of the Holy Spirit, so that they believe in God. And as we mentioned, this psalm was said at the Feast of Pentecost, on which the Holy Spirit descended in the New Testament.
